questions.problem: If $\operatorname{tan}⁡\alpha =0.70$ and $\alpha $ is acute, then the value of $\alpha $ in degrees to one decimal place is
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\alpha $ we use $arctan.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\alpha  & =0.70 \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡\alpha ) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0.70) \\ \alpha  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0.70)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using a calculator, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0.70) \\  & =(34.992\,0…)^{∘} \\  & ≈{35.0}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.problem: Mary has twelve different types of fruits. If she wants to choose three fruits without repetition, one for breakfast, one for lunch, and one for dinner, how many possible permutations of fruits does she have to choose from?
questions.worked_solution:
The number of permutations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{P}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}.
$$

There are $12$ pieces of fruit, so $n=12.$ We want to select $3$ of those fruits so we have $r=3.$

Therefore, the number of possible choices is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{12}{P}_{3} & =\frac{12!}{(12-3)!} \\  & =\frac{12!}{9!} \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 11\cdot 10\cdot \cancel{9!}}{\cancel{9!}} \\  & =12\cdot 11\cdot 10 \\  & =1\,320.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=4\sqrt[3]{x}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\sqrt[3]{x}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt[3]{x}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/3}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(8)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(8) & =\frac{4}{3\sqrt[3]{{8}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\sqrt[3]{64}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\cdot 4} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=\frac{1}{3}$ and the coordinates of our point $(8,8),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-8 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-8) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{8}{3}+8 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $5,\,10,\,15,\,…$

II. $3,\,18,\,108,\,…$

III. $-8,\,-24,\,-72,\,…$
questions.worked_solution:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{10}{5}=2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{15}{10}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{18}{3}=6 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{108}{18}=6\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is also geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-24)}{(-8)}=3 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-72)}{(-24)}=3\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequences II and III could be geometric sequences.

questions.problem: Find the formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is $9$ and the second term is $1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

$$
f(n)=f(1)+(n-1)d.
$$

We are given the first term $f(1)=9.$ Also, the common difference of the sequence can be found as

$$
d=1-9=-8.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)+(n-1)d \\  & =9+(n-1)(-8) \\  & =9-8n+8 \\  & =17-8n\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is $f(n)=17-8n.$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{2}-5x+6?$

I. $x=2$ is a root of $f(x)$

II. $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x)$

III. $(x-2)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder
questions.worked_solution:
The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x-2).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & =0 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We now check each of the statements, in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $x=2$ is a root of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & ={2}^{2}-5(2)+6 \\  & =4-10+6 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. According to the factor theorem, since $x=2$ is a root of $f(x),$ then $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x).$

- Statement III is true. Since $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ then $(x-2)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem: Given that the function $f(x)$ has an inverse ${f}^{-1}(x)$, and the point $(-4,\sqrt{3})$ lies on the graph $y=f(x),$ which point must lie on the graph of $y={f}^{-1}(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ is a reflection of $y=f(x)$ in the line $y=x.$ Therefore, each point $(a,b)$ on $y=f(x)$ has a corresponding point $(b,a)$ on $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ (the $x$ and $y$ coordinates swap).

Since the point $(-4,\sqrt{3})$ lies on $y=f(x),$ the point $(\sqrt{3},-4)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

questions.problem: Find the real solution to the equation $(x+2)^{3}=-8.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this equation by taking the $3$rd root of each side and solving for $x.$
Since $n=3$ is odd, there is only one real solution to this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{3} & =-8 \\ \sqrt[3]{(x+2)^{3}} & =\sqrt[3]{-8} \\ x+2 & =\sqrt[3]{(-2)^{3}} \\ x+2 & =-2 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-4.$
